segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul looked intently at the council and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience to this day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the law, and yet in violation of the law you order me to be struck?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those standing by said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I did not know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when Paul realized that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was split.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, while Pharisees affirm them all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A great outcry arose, and some of the scribes from the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended fiercely, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We find nothing wrong in this man. And if a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the dispute grew violent, the commander, afraid that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from their midst, and bring him into the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The following night the Lord stood by him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage! For as you have testified fully about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, declaring that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were more than forty who formed this conspiracy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went to the chief priests and the elders and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So now you, together with the council, notify the commander to bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine his case more closely. And we are ready to kill him before he gets near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the son of Paul’s sister heard of the ambush, and he came, entered the barracks, and reported it to Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul called one of the centurions and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take this young man to the commander, for he has something to report to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he took him, brought him to the commander, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to tell you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is it that you have to report to me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him. They have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him, and now they are ready, waiting for your consent.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the commander dismissed the young man, ordering him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell no one that you have notified me of this.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he called two of the centurions and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, to leave at the third hour of the night.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Provide mounts as well, so that they can put Paul on them and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he wrote a letter to this effect:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency the governor Felix: greetings.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman citizen.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I found that he was being accused over disputed points of their law, but that there was no charge against him deserving death or imprisonment.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, and I have also ordered his accusers to state their case against him before you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the soldiers, in accordance with their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day they let the horsemen go on with him and returned to the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the horsemen entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After reading it, he asked what province he was from, and on learning that he was from Cilicia,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I will give you a full hearing,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “when your accusers also arrive.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod’s palace.

notes.note: This is Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest from about AD 47 to the late 50s, not the Annas of the Gospels. Josephus portrays him as wealthy and grasping, and he was killed by Jewish insurgents at the outbreak of the revolt against Rome in AD 66.

The image is of a clean coat of plaster hiding something unsound or unclean beneath it. It echoes Ezekiel 13:10-15, where a flimsy wall daubed with whitewash is destined to fall, and resembles Jesus's ‘whitewashed tombs’ in Matthew 23:27. Paul's charge is that a judge who orders a blow before any verdict is himself breaking the law he claims to apply.

It is disputed whether Paul truly failed to recognise the high priest (the hearing was irregular and convened by a Roman officer) or is speaking with irony, implying that no one behaving this way could be taken for a high priest. The Greek allows either, and the translation leaves the question open. The quotation is from Exodus 22:28.

The Greek word normally means ‘both’, though three things have just been listed. In the Greek of this period it can be used loosely for more than two, which is the reading taken here. Others keep ‘both’ and understand two items: resurrection on the one hand, and angel-or-spirit on the other.

notes.traditional: let us not fight against God
notes.note: In the earliest manuscripts the sentence breaks off unfinished, as if drowned out by the uproar. Many later manuscripts complete it with ‘let us not fight against God’, probably borrowed from Acts 5:39, and the King James Version follows them. The text here follows the shorter reading.

The Greek title, literally ‘leader of a thousand’, was the standard equivalent for a Roman military tribune, here the officer commanding the cohort stationed in Jerusalem. His name, Claudius Lysias, appears in verse 26. The ‘barracks’ are generally identified with the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple courts, which is why the troops ‘go down’.

notes.traditional: bound themselves under a curse; bound themselves by an oath
notes.note: The verb means to call down a curse on oneself if a vow is not kept; in effect, ‘may God destroy us if we fail’. It is stronger than an ordinary oath, and verse 14 intensifies it further with a doubled expression.

notes.phrase: as though it were going to inquire
notes.note: Manuscripts differ over who is said to be about to inquire: the council (‘it’), the Jews (‘they’), or the commander (‘you’). The text translated here makes the council the subject. The pretext is the same in each case.

The meaning of this word is uncertain. It occurs nowhere else in surviving Greek until centuries later, and its form suggests something held in or taken by the right hand. ‘Spearmen’ is the traditional guess, and other proposals include light-armed troops or slingers; the translation keeps the traditional rendering for want of better evidence.

notes.phrase: the third hour of the night
notes.note: Night hours were counted from sunset, so this is roughly nine in the evening. The size of the escort, about half the Jerusalem garrison, shows how seriously the commander took the threat to a Roman citizen in his custody.

notes.phrase: having learned that he is a Roman citizen
notes.traditional: having understood that he was a Roman
notes.note: ‘Roman’ here means a holder of Roman citizenship, not a native of Rome. In Luke's narrative (21:31-33; 22:24-29) the commander discovered Paul's citizenship only after arresting him and ordering him flogged. The letter rearranges events to put its writer in a better light, and Luke lets the reader notice this.

The Greek borrows the Latin praetorium, the official residence and headquarters of a Roman governor. In Caesarea this was the palace built by Herod the Great, taken over by the Roman administration. ‘Palace’ is used because the building is identified by its builder; some translations keep ‘praetorium’ or use ‘headquarters’.

candidates.reason: Recurs through Acts 21-25 and in John 18:12, Mark 6:21 and Revelation, where translations vary between tribune, commander, chief captain and general.
Translations split between ‘council’ and the loanword ‘Sanhedrin’ across the Gospels and Acts, and readers would be confused if it varied.
Appears in the passion narratives, Acts and Philippians 1:13 and is variously rendered praetorium, palace, headquarters or imperial guard; a single policy is needed.

Very frequent in the Gospels and Acts; ‘scribes’ suggests copyists to a modern reader where the word means experts in the Jewish law, so one decision is needed between ‘scribes’, ‘teachers of the law’ and similar.
Common in Luke-Acts alongside ἀποκτείνω; a decision is needed whether to distinguish the two (‘do away with’ versus ‘kill’) or merge them.
